stem: What is a perceptron?
choices: A layer of trainable convolution matrices applied to a grid of pixels
A mathematical-computational model of a generic neuron: it sums weighted incoming signals and fires once the total passes an internal threshold
The compressed internal code at the narrowest point of an autoencoder
A rule that maps a symbol to a response, as in an expert system
explanation: A perceptron sums excitatory and inhibitory inputs, each scaled by a weight, and fires when that weighted sum exceeds its threshold. The convolution matrix is the CNN's building block, not the neuron.

stem: What does the P in MLP stand for?
explanation: Perceptron. MLP is Multilayer Perceptron, and the perceptron is the mathematical model of a generic neuron: it sums weighted incoming signals and fires when that sum exceeds an internal threshold.

stem: What is the difference between a perceptron and a multilayer perceptron?
choices: A perceptron learns from data; a multilayer perceptron has its weights set by hand
A perceptron handles images; a multilayer perceptron handles text
A perceptron is a single artificial neuron and can only separate linearly separable data; an MLP stacks layers of them, each layer's output feeding the next
A perceptron is biological; a multilayer perceptron is artificial
explanation: One perceptron draws one straight boundary, which is why XOR defeats it. Stacking layers is what buys the nonlinear decision boundaries, and in an MLP there is no recurrence and no skipping of layers.

stem: Why is XOR the classic argument for stacking layers of neurons?
choices: XOR requires more inputs than a single neuron can accept
XOR is not linearly separable, so no single straight boundary — and therefore no single perceptron — can compute it
XOR needs recurrence, because the output depends on previous inputs
XOR produces continuous outputs, and a perceptron produces only binary ones
explanation: AND and OR can each be separated by one straight line, so one perceptron suffices; XOR cannot, so you need a layer to bend the boundary. This is the limitation Minsky and Papert made famous in 1969.

stem: In a neuron's weighted sum, what job does the bias do that the weights do not?
choices: It scales each incoming signal according to how important that input is
It introduces the nonlinearity that lets the network learn curved boundaries
It normalises the inputs so they all lie on the same scale
It shifts the decision threshold — how large the weighted sum has to be before the neuron fires
explanation: Weights scale the inputs; the bias moves the threshold. Push the bias all the way up and the neuron becomes almost impossible to fire, which is exactly how it behaves as a decision threshold. The nonlinearity comes from the activation function, not the bias.

stem: One word: which parameter of a neuron shifts its decision threshold, as opposed to scaling an input?
explanation: The bias. Weights scale each incoming signal according to its importance; the bias shifts how large the weighted sum must be before the neuron fires, which is why the course states flatly that bias equals decision threshold.

stem: What makes up the trainable parameters of a single neuron with two inputs?
choices: One weight per input plus one bias for the neuron
One weight per input only — the bias is fixed before training
One weight for the whole neuron plus one bias per input
Two weights and two biases, one pair per input
explanation: Each incoming connection carries its own weight, and the neuron carries a single bias — so a two-input neuron has three trainable numbers. The inputs themselves are given data, not parameters.

stem: A student uses 'weight', 'coefficient', 'parameter', 'input' and 'hyperparameter' interchangeably. Which correction is right?
choices: All five mean the same thing in a neural network
Weight, coefficient and parameter are the same learned numbers; inputs are the x variables you supply; hyperparameters are set before training begins
Weight and coefficient are learned; parameter and hyperparameter are both set before training; inputs are outputs of the previous layer
Parameter and input are the same thing; weight, coefficient and hyperparameter are all learned
explanation: Weights, coefficients and parameters are three names for the numbers learned from data. Inputs are the x variables chosen by variable selection, and hyperparameters — layer count, learning rate — are fixed before training starts.

stem: What is the difference between variable selection and feature engineering?
choices: Variable selection happens during training; feature engineering happens after it
Variable selection reduces the number of layers; feature engineering increases it
Variable selection chooses which x variables to use; feature engineering builds a new input out of existing ones by a logical function, such as one variable divided by another
They are two names for the same preprocessing step
explanation: Selection picks from what you already have; engineering manufactures something new out of it. Both happen before training, which is why they are easy to confuse.

stem: What is the difference between a biological neural network and an artificial one?
choices: A BNN is the actual brain; an ANN is a mathematical model of it, and every modern AI is built from ANNs
A BNN learns; an ANN only stores rules that engineers wrote
A BNN has layers; an ANN has none
They are the same thing described at different levels of detail
explanation: The BNN is the real tissue; the ANN is the mathematical abstraction of how those neurons connect and communicate. The abstraction, not the biology, is what every modern AI system is actually built from.

stem: What distinguishes a feedforward network from a recurrent one?
choices: Feedforward networks are trained by backpropagation; recurrent ones are not trained at all
In a feedforward network the signal travels one way only; in a recurrent network it loops back into the network
Feedforward networks handle images; recurrent networks handle numbers
Feedforward networks have one layer; recurrent networks have many
explanation: The whole distinction is the direction of travel: forward only, or fed back in. An MLP is feedforward — no recurrence and no skipping over layers.

stem: What does a loss function actually return, and what is done with it?
choices: The network's confidence in its answer, which is reported to the user
A gradient vector, which is added directly to the weights
A single number measuring how far the output is from the ground truth, which training then minimises by adjusting weights and biases
A probability distribution over classes, from which the prediction is sampled
explanation: The loss is one number saying how wrong the network currently is — the course's phrase is that it tells you how far you are from the truth. Minimising it by gradient descent is the whole of training.

stem: How do a loss function and RMSE relate to each other?
choices: RMSE is the general notion of error; a loss function is one particular way of computing RMSE
The loss function L is the general 'how wrong am I' number, and RMSE — root mean squared error — is one specific choice of it
They are unrelated: RMSE measures accuracy, the loss function measures speed
RMSE is used for generative models, loss functions for predictive ones
explanation: L is the general object; RMSE is one instance, and cross-entropy is another used for classification. Saying 'the loss function is RMSE' is only right for the particular model that happens to use it.

stem: A gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent. What does gradient descent therefore do with it?
choices: Follows it, because the loss surface is inverted before training
Ignores it and searches randomly until the loss stops falling
Solves for the point where it equals zero, in a single analytic step
Takes a small step against it, then recomputes, repeating until the loss stops falling
explanation: Negate the gradient and you have the direction of steepest descent; the algorithm is stepwise and iterative, like a ball rolling down a surface. It is not a one-shot analytic solution, which is why it only ever reaches a local minimum.

stem: One word: what do you call the vector that gives the direction of steepest ascent of the loss, and which training steps against?
explanation: The gradient. It points uphill, so the algorithm negates it and takes a small step downhill, recomputes, and repeats — the ball-rolling-down-a-surface picture of training.

stem: State the relationship between gradient descent and backpropagation.
choices: Backpropagation is a specialisation of the gradient descent algorithm, applied to minimise prediction error for a multilayer perceptron by tweaking its weights and biases
Gradient descent is a specialisation of backpropagation, applied when the network has only one layer
They are alternative optimisers: you choose one or the other for a given network
Backpropagation computes the loss; gradient descent computes the prediction
explanation: That first sentence is the one to memorise verbatim. Gradient descent is the general 'step downhill' optimiser; backprop is what it becomes once the thing being optimised is a layered network and the error has to travel backwards through it.

stem: One word: name the algorithm that specialises gradient descent to a multilayer perceptron by sending prediction error backwards through the layers.
explanation: Backpropagation. The sentence to memorise: backpropagation is a specialisation of the gradient descent algorithm, applied to minimise prediction error for a multilayer perceptron by tweaking weights and biases.

stem: ADAM is named in the course as a refinement of plain gradient descent. What does the name stand for?
choices: Automatic Differentiation And Minimisation
Adaptive Descent Across Minima
Adaptive Moment Estimation
Averaged Directional Approximation Method
explanation: Adaptive Moment Estimation: it keeps running estimates of the gradient's moments so each parameter gets its own adapting step size, rather than one fixed step for all. It is still gradient descent underneath.

stem: Why did ReLU displace the sigmoid as the default activation in deep networks?
choices: Sigmoid outputs negative numbers, which networks cannot propagate
Sigmoid squashes everything into a narrow range, so gradients vanish as they pass back through many layers; ReLU passes positive values through untouched
ReLU is nonlinear and sigmoid is linear, so only ReLU can bend a decision boundary
ReLU can be computed in parallel on a GPU and sigmoid cannot
explanation: Both are nonlinear; the difference is the gradient. Sigmoid saturates, so the error signal shrinks towards nothing over many layers — the vanishing gradient problem — while ReLU returns its input when positive and zero otherwise, keeping the gradient alive and costing almost nothing to compute.

stem: Name the activation function, also called the ramp, that returns its input when positive and zero otherwise.
explanation: ReLU, the rectified linear unit — 'ramp' in Mathematica's vocabulary. It supplies cheap nonlinearity and, unlike the sigmoid, does not squash the gradient away in deep networks.

stem: What separates softmax from sigmoid?
choices: Softmax squashes a single value into the range 0 to 1; sigmoid turns a vector into class probabilities
Softmax is used during training, sigmoid only at inference time
Softmax turns a vector of raw activations into a probability distribution across classes that sums to 1; sigmoid squashes one value into the range 0 to 1
They compute the same thing; softmax is simply the faster implementation
explanation: Softmax is a whole-vector operation with the constraint that the outputs sum to one, which is what makes them class probabilities. Sigmoid acts on one number at a time and carries no such constraint.

stem: In the canonical handwritten-digit network, what happens across successive layers?
choices: Each layer repeats the same computation, and depth only adds numerical precision
Raw pixels become edges, edges become patterns such as loops and strokes, and the final layer identifies the digit
The first layer identifies the digit and later layers check that answer
Each layer discards a fixed fraction of the pixels until only the digit remains
explanation: Depth buys hierarchical abstraction: pixels to edges to patterns to identity. It is the same hierarchy Hubel and Wiesel found in the cat — lines, then curves, then shapes, then objects.

stem: A trained network reaches high accuracy on its test set. What does the course warn you not to conclude from that?
choices: That it will run fast enough to deploy
That the training data was large enough
That it has found a human-like abstraction of the problem — it has only settled into one local minimum of the loss surface that happens to work
That the loss function was correctly chosen
explanation: Gradient descent finds a local minimum, not the truth. High accuracy means the parameters work on the data you have, not that the network has learned the concept the way a person would.

stem: What does the universal approximation result say, and what does it not say?
choices: It says a neural network can represent very complex mappings; it does not say that training will find the right parameters, which still needs data, architecture, optimisation and regularisation
It says any network will converge to the global minimum given enough steps
It says every function can be learned exactly with enough training data
It says deeper networks always outperform shallower ones
explanation: Universal approximation establishes representational capacity only — the function is in there somewhere. Finding it is a separate, empirical problem, which is why the infographic pairs it with gradient-based learning as the other half of the common AI engine.

stem: Deep learning names a genuinely new architecture, unrelated to the multilayer perceptron of the 1980s.
choices: True
False
explanation: False. The course glossary calls deep learning a modern rebranding of the MLP; what changed was the compute available, the algorithmic tweaks that stop weights degenerating across many layers, and the size of the datasets.

stem: What is one-hot encoding?
choices: Scaling every input so it lies between 0 and 1
Representing a category as a list of slots in which exactly one is on and all the rest are off
Turning a word into a dense vector of several hundred numbers
Discarding the least useful input variables before training
explanation: One slot lit out of ten, like the digit displays in the course's example. It is the opposite of an embedding, which is dense and learned and puts similar items close together; a one-hot vector says nothing about similarity.

stem: How is overfitting detected?
choices: The training error stops falling while the validation error keeps improving
Both the training error and the validation error stay high
The training error keeps falling while the validation error plateaus or starts rising
The loss oscillates instead of decreasing smoothly
explanation: Overfitting is the gap opening between the two curves: the model keeps fitting the training set better while generalising worse. Both errors staying high is underfitting — the model simply lacks capacity.

stem: How many hidden layers does the universal approximation theorem actually require?
choices: One
Two
At least three
It depends on the number of inputs
explanation: One hidden layer with finitely many neurons suffices to approximate any continuous function on a closed bounded region to any tolerance. Depth is not needed for expressive power — it is needed because deep networks reach the same expressivity with far fewer parameters and are easier to optimise.

stem: 'Expressivity is abundant; trainability is scarce.' What does that claim mean in practice?
choices: Networks can represent almost anything, but finding the parameters that do is the hard part, which is why architecture and optimisation choices matter
Networks can be trained easily but cannot represent complex functions
Larger networks are always easier to train than smaller ones
The theory shows training will converge, so only the data matter
explanation: Universal approximation says the function is in there somewhere; it says nothing about whether gradient descent will find it. Design choices — skip connections, functional links, architectures — are inductive biases that make good solutions reachable.

stem: A network can be given higher functional complexity in three complementary ways. Which set is right?
choices: More data, more epochs, more regularisation
More classes, more features, more labels
Wider layers, larger batches, smaller learning rates
Enrich what the links compute, create many computational paths, and make the network deep
explanation: Functional links enrich what each connection computes; residual connections create many alternative paths; sequential stacking adds depth. They are three answers to one question — how to represent a rich set of functions — and they can be combined.

stem: A functional-link network raises a shallow network's power without adding depth. How?
choices: By adding explicit nonlinear transforms of the inputs — polynomial, radial-basis or trigonometric terms — so the basis the network works from is richer
By adding identity shortcuts between layers
By dropping units at random during training
By sharing weights across positions in the input
explanation: The functional link puts hand-chosen nonlinear features in alongside the raw inputs, which works well with little data when you know what features matter. Its cost is that you need that prior knowledge, and the input dimension can grow large.

stem: By early 2015 making networks deeper had stopped working. What exactly was going wrong?
choices: The networks were overfitting, so training error fell while validation error rose

Beyond roughly twenty to thirty layers accuracy stalled and then got worse — a deeper model scored a higher training error than a shallower one, so it was an optimisation failure rather than overfitting
The networks ran out of memory on the available hardware
The labels in ImageNet had become too noisy
explanation: This is the degradation problem, and the giveaway is that the deeper model was worse on the training set too. Overfitting would have shown as a widening gap between training and validation, not as a worse fit to the data it had seen.

stem: Why was the degradation problem so confounding to the researchers who found it?
choices: No one had a dataset large enough to test it
The deeper networks had fewer parameters than the shallower ones
A deeper network could always match a shallower one by making its extra layers identity mappings, so the solution provably existed — the optimiser simply could not find it
It only appeared on one dataset and could not be reproduced
explanation: Add sixteen pass-through layers to a trained fourteen-layer model and performance should be at least as good. That solution sits in the parameter space and gradient descent never reaches it, which is what identified the problem as optimisation rather than capacity.

stem: One word: the kind of connection that adds a layer's input back to its output, so the layers learn a correction rather than the whole mapping.
explanation: A residual connection, also called a shortcut. Instead of learning H(x) directly the block learns F(x) = H(x) − x, so the output is F(x) + x — refining rather than re-creating.

stem: What does a residual block learn, and why is that easier?
choices: It learns the full mapping H(x) twice and averages the two
It learns a separate weight for every input position
It learns to discard x and rebuild it from the layer below
It learns the residual F(x) = H(x) − x, so the output is F(x) + x — the block only has to learn the correction, and doing nothing is available by construction
explanation: Refine rather than re-create. If the best thing a block can do is leave the signal alone, it needs only to drive F(x) to zero, which is a far easier target than reproducing the identity through a stack of weight layers.

stem: One influential reading is that residual networks behave like ensembles of relatively shallow networks. What is the argument?
choices: Each residual block is trained separately and the results averaged

A network with L residual blocks contains 2^L implicit input-output paths, since each block may be used or skipped; most of those paths are short, and almost all of the gradient comes from the short ones
The network is duplicated L times and the copies vote
Residual networks are trained on L different subsets of the data
explanation: Unravel the shortcuts and a 110-block network turns out to train mostly through paths of ten to thirty-odd blocks. Effective depth during training is much smaller than nominal depth, which is why very deep residual nets train at all.

stem: Do skip connections change what functions a network can represent, or how easily it can be trained?
choices: They change what it can represent: without them the network is not a universal approximator
They change neither; they only reduce memory use
They change how easily it can be trained — they reshape the optimisation landscape and the effective depth, while the class of functions available was already unrestricted
They change both equally
explanation: Universal approximation already held for a plain network, so expressivity was never the obstacle. The shortcut is an inductive bias that makes good solutions findable, which is the practical distinction between what a model could do and what training will actually deliver.

stem: Backpropagation is usually credited to Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams in 1986. What is the fuller attribution?
choices: Werbos published the method in a 1974 doctoral dissertation; the 1986 paper made it widely known and showed it worked on useful networks
Rosenblatt published it in 1958 and the 1986 paper corrected an error in it
Cybenko published it in 1989, after the 1986 paper
Minsky and Papert published it in 1969 as a response to their own criticism
explanation: Werbos had the algorithm in 1974; the 1986 Nature paper is where it entered the field. The distinction matters for a names-and-dates question: 1986 is the popularisation, not the invention.

stem: What does the chain rule do for backpropagation?
choices: It guarantees that the loss will reach zero
It converts the loss surface into a convex one
It chooses the learning rate automatically
It lets the derivative of the loss with respect to a deep weight be assembled from a product of local derivatives, so one backward sweep yields the gradient for every weight in the network
explanation: A feedforward network is a composition of functions, and the chain rule differentiates a composition. That is the whole trick: without it you would have to perturb each weight separately, which for thirteen thousand weights would be hopeless and for a billion impossible.

stem: In training a network, what is computed on the forward pass and what on the backward pass?
choices: Forward computes the gradients; backward computes the prediction
Forward computes the activations layer by layer to produce the prediction and hence the loss; backward computes the gradients of that loss with respect to every weight
Forward computes the loss; backward computes the learning rate
Both compute the same quantities, once in each direction, as a check
explanation: Forward: activations and loss. Backward: gradients. Gradient descent then uses those gradients to update the weights — backprop computes the direction, gradient descent takes the step.

stem: In the gradient descent update rule, what is the learning rate?
choices: The proportion of the training data used at each step
The rate at which the loss is guaranteed to fall
The number of passes made over the training set
The step size that multiplies the gradient, deciding how far the parameters move each iteration
explanation: It is a hyperparameter, set before training rather than learned. Too small and training crawls; too large and the update overshoots the valley it was meant to descend.

stem: Batch, stochastic, mini-batch, momentum, RMSProp and Adam are all listed as one kind of thing. Which of these does not belong on that list?
choices: Momentum
RMSProp
Mini-batch
Backpropagation
explanation: The others are variants of gradient descent, differing in how much data each step uses or how the step size adapts. Backpropagation is not an alternative to them — it is how the gradient they all consume gets computed.

stem: In the canonical handwritten-digit network, how is the cost function defined?
choices: The sum of squared differences between the actual output activations and the desired ones, averaged over tens of thousands of training examples
The largest single output activation, which should be close to one
The number of digits misclassified in the test set
The distance between the input image and the reconstructed image
explanation: One example gives a squared-error measure of how lousy the output is; the cost is that averaged over the whole training set. Training then means adjusting the weights and biases to bring that single number down.

stem: A network taking a 28 by 28 image into 784 input neurons, through two hidden layers of 16, to 10 outputs has roughly how many weights and biases to tune?
choices: About 800
About 13,000
About 150,000
About 2 million
explanation: Roughly thirteen thousand knobs and dials, dominated by the 784 by 16 first layer. Training is the search for a setting of all of them at once, which is why it is done by gradient descent rather than by hand.

stem: The loss surface of a neural network is bowl-shaped, so gradient descent is guaranteed to reach the global minimum.
choices: True
False
explanation: False. The surface is high-dimensional and non-convex, full of local minima and saddle points, and gradient descent settles in a local minimum. The practical finding is that in high dimensions those local minima are usually good enough.

stem: A single neuron takes three inputs. How many trainable parameters does it have?
choices: Three
Four
Six
Seven
explanation: Three weights, one per input, plus one bias — four in all. The rule to carry into the exam: one weight per incoming connection plus one bias per neuron, and the inputs themselves are data, not parameters.

stem: A layer of three neurons each receives the same four inputs. How many trainable parameters does that layer hold?
choices: Twelve
Fifteen
Seven
Sixteen
explanation: Four weights for each of the three neurons is twelve, plus one bias each is three — fifteen. Forgetting the biases is the standard slip, and it costs you three here.

stem: A network takes two inputs into a hidden layer of two neurons, then into a single output neuron. How many parameters must training tune?
choices: Six
Seven
Nine
Twelve
explanation: Hidden layer: two neurons times two weights plus two biases is six. Output: two weights plus one bias is three. Six and three is nine. Count layer by layer and add the biases as you go.

stem: When you count a network's parameters, which things count and which do not?
choices: Weights and biases count because they are learned; the inputs are given data and the hyperparameters are fixed before training, so neither counts
Weights, biases and inputs all count, because all three are numbers the network uses
Only the weights count; a bias is a constant and is not trained
Weights, biases and hyperparameters count, because all three affect the output
explanation: A parameter is something training changes. That excludes the x values you supply and the learning rate or layer count you chose in advance — which is the same weight-versus-input-versus-hyperparameter distinction in a different disguise.

stem: A hard threshold fires or does not fire. Why is it replaced by a smooth S-shaped function?
choices: To make the neuron faster to evaluate
To let the neuron accept negative inputs
To keep the output bounded between zero and one for interpretation as a probability, only
To make the model differentiable, so its parameters can be tuned by gradient-based learning — a step has no useful derivative
explanation: A step function's derivative is zero everywhere it exists, so gradient descent has nothing to follow. Smoothing the edge is what makes the whole architecture learnable, which is why the optimization principle depends on it.

stem: The bias is often written as a weight w₀ attached to an input x₀ that is permanently set to 1. Why bother?
choices: It lets the bias be trained while the weights are frozen
It makes the bias act as a learning rate
It folds the bias into the weight vector, so the neuron's whole computation becomes one dot product of weights against inputs
It prevents the bias from growing too large
explanation: A tidy bookkeeping trick, not a change of substance: with x₀ = 1 the sum of weights times inputs already includes the bias. The bias still does its own job — shifting the decision threshold — and still counts as a parameter.

stem: A one-dimensional line separates a two-dimensional plane. A dataset with thirty input variables is separated by what?
choices: A thirty-dimensional hyperplane
A twenty-nine-dimensional hyperplane
A one-dimensional line, as always
A thirty-one-dimensional hyperplane
explanation: The separating surface always has one dimension fewer than the space it cuts: n − 1. The picture generalises exactly — what changes with dimension is only how impossible it becomes to draw.

stem: A classifier's threshold is moved so that fewer cases are flagged. A civil court would want that; a military command would not. What does the contrast show?
choices: That false positives are errors and false negatives are not
That accuracy is the only figure that matters
That moving the threshold removes errors altogether
That false positives and false negatives are both errors but cost different amounts, so the threshold is set by which error you can least afford
explanation: A civil court would rather let a guilty party go than punish an innocent one, so it minimises false positives; a military command would rather investigate a harmless contact than miss a real one, so it minimises false negatives. No placement of the boundary eliminates both.
